newsitem.title: CANADA: Cholesterol control keeps bypass arteries open.
newsitem.headline: Cholesterol control keeps bypass arteries open.

text.p: Cutting "bad" cholesterol by 25 to 47 percent can significantly extend the length of time that heart bypass surgery is effective, according to a study published in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.
The research examined the speed with which veins, taken from the leg and stitched into the heart to bypass clogged arteries, eventually become clogged themselves by new cholesterol deposits.
The problem is important because, within 10 to 12 years after surgery, cholesterol has narrowed 30 to 40 percent of the bypass grafts, past research has shown.
Aggressive cholesterol control can reduce that percentage significantly, but administering medicine that prevents blood clots does not help new heart vessels stay open longer, the study suggests.

"This study provides a definitive answer to the question of whether coronary bypass grafts respond to cholesterol lowering," said Dr. Claude Lenfant, director of the Canadian National Heart, Lung and Blood Institute, which funded the test.

Dr. Lucien Campeau, senior cardiologist at the Montreal Heart Institute and chairman of the clinical trial, said low cholesterol diets only reduce cholesterol levels in heart disease patients by three to four percent.

To reduce cholesterol levels by the 30 to 35 percent needed to prolong the benefits of heart bypass surgery, intensive treatment with cholesterol-lowering agents was needed, he told a news conference.
"Primary physicians are somewhat afraid to use it, but with time they will learn that it is a very safe drug," he said.
The anti-cholesterol drugs used in the study were lovastatin, sold under the brand name Mevacor by Merck & Co and cholestyramine, sold under the brand name Questran by Bristol-Myers Squibb.

Campeau said it was astonishing that only a fraction of coronary patients actually knew what their cholesterol levels were. That information, and steps taken to significantly lower those levels, would help eliminate many patients' need for second heart bypass operations.

Of the 15,000 heart bypass operations each year in Canada, about 10 percent are re-operations, Campeau said. About one million such surgeries are done in the United States annually at a cost of over US$15 billion.
"If we can reduce that number by 40 percent I think that is quite a saving," Campeau said.

The team of U.S. and Canadian researchers studied 1,351 volunteers. Some were given enough medicine to bring their levels of "bad" cholesterol -- also known as low density lipoprotein, or LDL -- below 95 milligrams per deciliter of blood. The rest received enough medication to drop their cholesterol levels to less than 140.
The National Cholesterol Education Program advises people with heart disease to lower their levels of "bad" cholesterol to below 100.
The patients also were instructed to take either a placebo or the anti-clotting drug warfarin.
At the beginning of the study and about four years later, doctors measured the size of the opening of the bypass grafts.

They found 39 percent of the grafts had started to clog in patients whose cholesterol levels had fallen by a moderate amount, compared with 27 percent of the grafts among those who got the larger dose of anti-cholesterol medicine.
The warfarin treatment made no difference. Warfarin is the generic name for Coumadin, sold by DuPont Pharma, a subsidiary of DuPont Merck, a privately-held company.
